hook.text: After the 2010 oil spill BP spent $500 million on ads—not cleanup, just reputation repair.

buildup.text: Corporate honor works like family honor: one scandal stains every employee and every product.

discovery.text: Reputation management is now a $5 billion industry. Companies hire firms to bury bad search results.

twist.text: Volkswagen's emissions scandal hurt German engineering's brand globally—one company shaming an entire nation.

climax.text: In the attention economy, corporate honor is the most valuable and fragile asset on the balance sheet.

punchline.text: Brands live and die by the same honor rules as clans.

quiz.question: How much did BP spend on reputation ads after the 2010 spill?

details.summary: Corporate honor operates through brand reputation — companies sue for defamation, fight hostile reviews, manage PR crises, and engage in competitive attacks. A damaged brand reputation can destroy billions in market value overnight.
details.whyItMatters: Corporate reputation wars show that honor culture never disappeared — it migrated from individuals and families to institutions. Understanding corporate honor dynamics explains PR crises, brand management, and competitive strategy.
takeaways: Brand damage can destroy billions in market value within hours
Corporate defamation lawsuits protect institutional honor
Reputation management is a multi-billion dollar industry

faq.question: How do corporations defend their honor?
faq.answer: Through legal action (defamation suits, injunctions), public relations (crisis management, apology campaigns), competitive attacks (undermining rival brands), and digital reputation management (SEO manipulation, review monitoring).

faq.question: Is corporate reputation really like personal honor?
faq.answer: Structurally, yes. Both operate on social perception rather than objective reality. Both can be destroyed by public exposure of transgression. Both require active maintenance through visible virtuous behavior. Both demand response to perceived insults.
